# Gasoline price. Data by Countries from 1995 to 2026

Authorization is required. Log In

 | Overview (Jun 17, 2026) 

 Global gasoline price trajectories diverged significantly in 2026. As of May 2026, the world's highest fuel prices were concentrated in developed city-states and EU countries, while the lowest prices remained in oil-exporting nations of the Persian Gulf as well as selected countries in Latin America and Asia. The five countries with the highest gasoline prices in 2026 were: Hong Kong at $4.17 per liter (+21.2% vs. 2025; +119.5% vs. 2010), Singapore at $3.39 (+19.8%; +138.7% vs. 2010), Israel at $2.94 (+44.8%; +59.0% vs. 2010), the Netherlands at $2.93 (+22.1%; +184.5% vs. 2000), and Denmark at $2.68 (+25.2%; +165.3% vs. 2000). The five countries with the lowest gasoline prices were: Venezuela at $0.01 per liter (0% vs. 2025; comparison with the 2020 baseline is not meaningful due to a zero-base effect), Kuwait at $0.28 (0%; +33.3% vs. 2000), Iran at $0.36 (0%; +63.6% vs. 2000), Egypt at $0.43 (+22.9%; +26.5% vs. 2015), and Malaysia at $0.50 (+4.2%; +78.6% vs. 2000). 

 The sharpest year-over-year increase was recorded in Lebanon, where gasoline prices rose from $0.78 per liter in 2025 to $1.44 in 2026 (+84.6%). Significant increases were also observed in Slovakia, where prices reached $2.06 (+57.3%), Israel at $2.94 (+44.8%), the United Arab Emirates at $0.97 (+44.8%), Nigeria at $0.93 (+43.1%), and the United States at $1.18 (+42.2%). Broad-based fuel price inflation was evident on both sides of the Atlantic in 2026, with increases recorded in the United Kingdom ($2.14; +19.6% vs. 2025), Germany ($2.33; +18.3%), France ($2.43; +22.7%), Italy ($2.38; +17.2%), as well as Canada ($1.38; +29.0%) and the United States ($1.18; +42.2%). 

 Over the past quarter-century, the largest price increases have been recorded in Central and Eastern Europe. Prices rose to $1.99 in Romania (+332.6% vs. 2000), $2.30 in Albania (+303.5%), $2.10 in Estonia (+250.0%), $2.48 in Greece (+244.4%), and $2.08 in Lithuania (+215.2%). At the same time, some markets experienced downward corrections: in Iceland, gasoline prices fell to $1.85 (−23.9% vs. 2025), while in Japan they declined to $1.06 (−14.5%). 

 Since the mid-1990s, the most pronounced synchronized global fuel price surges occurred in 2004 (following the post-2002 rebound), in 2010 and 2012 (when many countries reached new highs), and again during 2023–2026, when prices resumed climbing after the pandemic-driven collapse of 2020. The most significant global declines occurred in 2015 and 2020, when fuel prices fell simultaneously across a large number of markets.
